title: SHE HAD FIVE HUSBANDS… THEN JESUS MET HER BESIDE A WELL
paragraphs: SHE HAD FIVE HUSBANDS… THEN JESUS MET HER BESIDE A WELL
She came carrying a water jar. She walked away carrying a testimony. And somewhere between the two, Jesus touched the part of her life she probably wished nobody knew.
She did not know that an ordinary trip for water was about to become the day her story collided with the Messiah.
She came to a well.
Jesus was already there.

And before this encounter was over, He would speak about her thirst, expose the truth about her relationships, reveal the kind of worship the Father seeks, identify Himself as the Messiah, and turn a woman with a complicated past into someone running toward other people with news about Christ.
But there is something important we need to settle before we enter her story.
Scripture never tells us her name.
It never tells us why all five marriages ended.
It never explicitly says that all five endings were caused by her sexual sin.
Some may have ended through death. Some through divorce. Some through abandonment. We simply are not told.
So we should not accuse her of sins the Bible does not accuse her of committing.
What Scripture does tell us is startling enough.
Jesus knew her entire relational history.
Five husbands.
And the man she was currently with was not her husband.
Yet Jesus stayed.
That may be the first sentence somebody reading this needs to hear.
Jesus knew the truth before He started the conversation.
He was not gradually discovering who she was.
She was gradually discovering who He was.

John tells us that Jesus came to a Samaritan town called Sychar, near the field Jacob had given to Joseph. Jacob's well was there. Jesus, tired from His journey, sat beside it. It was about the sixth hour.
Then a Samaritan woman arrived to draw water.
Jesus said:
“Give me a drink.”
She was surprised.
“You are a Jew and I am a Samaritan woman. How can you ask me for a drink?”
John explains why the moment was so unusual: Jews and Samaritans did not normally associate freely with one another.
There were ethnic and religious tensions behind this conversation.
There were centuries behind this conversation.
There were social boundaries behind this conversation.
And yet Jesus spoke to her.
Before we turn this woman into a symbol, notice the humanity of the scene.
Jesus is tired.
There is a well.
There is a woman.
There is a conversation.
And there is a Savior who refuses to let human hostility determine whom He will address.
Jesus answered her by turning the conversation from the water beneath them to the thirst within her.
If she understood the gift of God and who was speaking to her, He said, she would have asked Him, and He would have given her living water.
She was confused.
The well was deep.
Jesus had no bucket.
How could this stranger possibly offer better water than Jacob's well?
Then Jesus moved beneath the surface.
The person drinking ordinary water would thirst again.
But the water He gives becomes within a person a spring rising toward eternal life.
She wanted it.
Of course she did.
“Give me this water.”
And then Jesus said something that seems, at first, like a sudden change of subject:
“Go, call your husband, and come here.”
There it is.
The sentence that opened the locked room.
The conversation moved from thirst...
to truth.
She answered:
“I have no husband.”
Technically true.
Painfully incomplete.
Jesus replied that she had spoken correctly.
Then came the words she could not have expected this stranger to know.
The Greek text of John 4:18 reads:
πέντε γὰρ ἄνδρας ἔσχες, καὶ νῦν ὃν ἔχεις οὐκ ἔστιν σου ἀνήρ
Pente gar andras esches, kai nyn hon echeis ouk estin sou anēr.
In straightforward English:
“For you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband.”
That is what the text actually says.
Notice what Jesus does not do.
He does not pretend her situation is something it isn't.
Grace does not require Jesus to rename darkness as light.
But He also does not humiliate her for entertainment.
Truth and mercy are standing beside the same well.
That is Jesus.
Some of us want a Christ who comforts us without confronting us.
Others imagine a Christ who confronts without compassion.
John gives us neither caricature.
Jesus offers living water...
and Jesus tells the truth.
Because the Savior who loves you too much to abandon you is also the Savior who loves you too much to leave your deepest thirst untouched.
Maybe that is why this story feels uncomfortable.
Because most of us have our own version of:
“I have no husband.”
Not necessarily the same sin.
Not necessarily the same circumstances.
But that carefully edited sentence we use when we want to tell enough truth to avoid technically lying while keeping the painful part safely hidden.
“I’m fine.”
“It wasn't that serious.”
“I can stop whenever I want.”
“Nobody knows.”
“My marriage is okay.”
“My prayer life is okay.”
“I forgave them.”
“I don't struggle with that anymore.”
“I only look sometimes.”
“I'll repent later.”
“God understands.”
And perhaps He does understand far more deeply than we realize.
But His understanding is not permission to keep hiding.
He knows.
The browser history.
The private messages.
The bitterness you keep feeding.
The relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
The secret addiction.
The pride underneath your ministry.
The jealousy behind the smile.
The compromise nobody at church sees.
The wounds you cover with jokes.
The nights when everyone thinks you are sleeping but you are staring into the darkness wondering how your life became this.
He knows.
And the frightening beauty of the Gospel is that the One who knows is still the One offering living water.
The woman recognized that something extraordinary was happening.
“Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet.”
The conversation turned toward worship.
Her people worshiped on Mount Gerizim. The Jews identified Jerusalem as the proper place of worship.
Jesus did not merely choose a side in an old religious argument. He announced something enormous.
The hour was coming—and had now arrived—when true worshipers would worship the Father in spirit and truth.
The Greek is beautiful:
ἐν πνεύματι καὶ ἀληθείᾳ
en pneumati kai alētheia
“in spirit and truth.”
And Jesus says:
ὁ πατὴρ τοιούτους ζητεῖ
ho patēr toioutous zētei
“the Father seeks such people.”
The Father is seeking worshipers.
Think about where Jesus chose to teach this.
Not inside a palace.
Not before an impressive religious audience.
Beside a well.
To a Samaritan woman whose relational history Jesus had just uncovered.
That should destroy the lie that your past automatically makes you unreachable.
But do not twist grace into another lie.
Jesus does not say that our past does not matter.
He demonstrates something better:
Our past does not have to have the final word when we encounter Him.
Christianity is not the announcement that sin is insignificant.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that reconciliation with God required something we could never accomplish for ourselves.
The Son of God came for sinners. Christ bore sin, died, and rose again. Forgiveness is not God pretending our rebellion never mattered. Forgiveness comes to us at immeasurable cost through Christ.
This is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is what happens when grace makes hiding unnecessary.
You stop defending what Christ died to forgive.
You stop calling bondage freedom.
You stop negotiating with the thing destroying you.
You bring it into His light.
Not because cleaning yourself up earns salvation.
It doesn't.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works.
But the grace that saves does not make peace with the chains from which Christ came to free us.
Then the woman said something that changed the atmosphere of the conversation.
She knew Messiah was coming—the One called Christ.
When He came, she said, He would explain everything.
And Jesus answered:
Ἐγώ εἰμι, ὁ λαλῶν σοι.
Egō eimi, ho lalōn soi.
Literally:
“I am, the one speaking to you.”
In context, Jesus is identifying Himself to her as the Messiah she has been waiting for.
Imagine that moment.
Five husbands were no longer the biggest fact in the story.
The man she was currently with was no longer the biggest fact in the story.
Her ethnicity was not the biggest fact.
Her complicated history was not the biggest fact.
Her shame—whatever form it took—was not the biggest fact.
The Messiah was standing in front of her.
And that is where scandal begins surrendering to grace.
Not because the scandal magically becomes good.
Not because consequences disappear.
Not because truth is rewritten.
But because Jesus can rewrite what happens next.
Then the disciples returned.
And John gives us one tiny detail that feels almost cinematic.
The woman left her water jar.
She had come because she needed water.
Now the jar was sitting beside the well while she hurried back toward the town.
John does not tell us exactly why she left it, so we should resist inventing certainty where Scripture gives none.
But the contrast is unforgettable.
She arrived focused on water.
She left talking about Jesus.
She told the people:
“Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did. Can this be the Christ?”
Do you see what happened?
The very knowledge that could have terrified her became part of her testimony.
He knew.
And she ran toward people instead of disappearing from them.
“Come and see.”
Not:
“Come meet a man who thinks I'm perfect.”
Not:
“Come meet a man who never discovered my history.”
But essentially:
Come meet the One who knows me.
There is freedom in being fully known by Christ and discovering that His invitation still stands.
The townspeople came.
And later many Samaritans believed, first because of the woman's testimony and then because they heard Jesus themselves.
They eventually confessed that He truly was “the Savior of the world.”
The woman who began the chapter talking about a bucket became a witness pointing people toward the Savior. John explicitly says that many Samaritans believed because of her testimony.
Do not miss that.
Her testimony did not save them.
Jesus did.
She was not the living water.
Jesus was.
She was not the Messiah.
Jesus was.
She simply pointed thirsty people toward the One she had encountered.
And perhaps that is where this stops being her story and starts becoming ours.
What if the thing you are most ashamed for anyone to know is the very place where Christ wants truth to replace hiding?
What if you have spent years trying to satisfy spiritual thirst from wells that cannot hold enough water?
Another relationship.
Another purchase.
Another promotion.
Another body.
Another screen.
Another secret.
Another round of applause.
Another person telling you that you matter.
Another Sunday appearance while your private life is collapsing.
Drink.
Thirst.
Drink.
Thirst.
Drink.
Thirst.
Jesus said ordinary water cannot permanently satisfy.
And neither can the substitutes we keep lowering into the wells of this world.
You can have thousands of followers and still be thirsty.
You can sleep beside somebody and still be thirsty.
You can preach and still be thirsty.
You can know Christian vocabulary and still be thirsty.
You can own a Bible and still be thirsty.
You can have money, sex, attention, influence, achievements, entertainment and everything your younger self thought would finally make you whole...
and discover at midnight that your soul is still standing beside an empty well.
Because the deepest thirst of the human heart cannot be healed by another created thing taking the place of the Creator.
You need Christ.
Not merely Christianity as culture.
Not merely inspirational quotations.
Not merely religious content.
Christ.
The crucified and risen Son of God.
The Savior who tells the truth.
The Savior who receives repentant sinners.
The Savior who forgives.
The Savior who gives eternal life.
The Savior who does not merely improve sinners but reconciles them to God and begins transforming them.
Maybe you have had your own five husbands.
Maybe not literally.
Maybe yours has five different names.
Approval.
Pornography.
Money.
Bitterness.
Control.
Or perhaps your deepest wound is something done to you, and you have wrongly carried shame for another person's sin.
Do not force every wound into the category of personal guilt.
Some things require repentance.
Other things require healing.
Many lives contain both.
Jesus knows the difference.
Bring Him the truth.
If you have sinned, repent and believe the Gospel.
If you have been wounded, bring that wound to the Savior rather than believing it has made you worthless.
If you have wandered, come home.
If you have become spiritually numb, ask Him to awaken you.
If you have been pretending, stop performing.
There is no advantage in hiding from the One who already knows.
And if these words exposed something you have kept buried, you do not need to write the details publicly.

And if Christ has already brought you through something you once thought would destroy you, tell someone what His grace has done. Your testimony does not need to make you the hero. Let Jesus be the Hero.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover that restoration is possible.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be walking toward the same empty well tonight.
Send this to the friend who has slowly disappeared.
And there is more than merchandise here.
It is not purchasing spiritual status.
It cannot earn salvation.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Not because an algorithm deserves your obedience.
Because somebody may need the message.
There may be a woman carrying her jar.
A man carrying his secret.
A believer barely holding onto faith.
A prodigal afraid to come home.
A skeptic who thinks Jesus only wants respectable people.
A wounded person convinced their history has disqualified them.
Let them see the well.
Let them hear the conversation.
Let them discover the Christ who already knows.
Because that woman was not transformed by finding a better hiding place.
She encountered Someone greater than her history.
Jesus knew about the five husbands before she said a word about them.
He knew about the man who was not her husband.
He knew her theology.
He knew her questions.
He knew her thirst.
And still He spoke.
Still He offered living water.
Still He revealed Himself.
Still He allowed her story to become a doorway through which others came to hear Him.
That is grace.
Not God pretending there was never a scandal.
Grace is Jesus entering the story and refusing to let sin, shame, brokenness, or yesterday be the final author.
So when your past whispers, You are what you did...
when shame whispers, Hide...
when religion whispers, Clean yourself up before you come...
remember the woman beside Jacob's well.
She came carrying a jar.
She left carrying news of Jesus.
And perhaps the most unforgettable thing about her story is not that she had five husbands.
It is that after Jesus revealed that He knew her story, He kept talking to her about eternal life.
The deepest miracle beside that well was not that Jesus knew her past—it was that her past already knew its final word had arrived, and His name was Jesus.
